logline: A prosecutor wakes up on death row with no memory of the crime that put him there, and must piece together the truth before his execution - while a corrupt doppelganger has stolen his identity and family.

bollymeter.basis: Ji Sung's committed lead performance drives this amnesia thriller to consistent ratings above 25 percent nationwide, peaking at 26.6 percent for the finale. Critics praised the propulsive premise while noting the show's reliance on repetitive twist cycles to sustain tension.

pull_quotes.text: A warning sign to the evil and powerful figures of the real world.

seasons.review_body: Defendant aired on SBS from January 23 to March 21, 2017, and became one of that year's dominant ratings performers, consistently exceeding 25 percent viewership and closing with a 26.6 percent nationwide average - the second-highest-rated SBS miniseries of 2017. The premise is a high-concept hook: a prosecutor wakes up as a death row inmate with total amnesia, pursued by a twin who has usurped his life. Ji Sung's dual registers - terrified victim and scheming antagonist, embodied by Um Ki-joon - gave the series its emotional engine. The Korea Times praised it as a real-world allegory for impunity among the powerful. Critics tempered enthusiasm with observations that the narrative recycled its twist mechanics, introducing new revelations on a near-episode basis to maintain momentum rather than deepening character. The 8.0 IMDb rating reflects a thriller that delivered on spectacle and performance while coasting on formula.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Defendant S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The court lets **David Collins** walk. The prosecution offers no further evidence, the old case collapses in public, and a man once imprisoned for his wife’s murder is free to leave. The hour does not treat that freedom as relief. It treats it as a problem everyone else must now solve. David wants justice and his children. The police want distance from their earlier work. The family wants safety, preferably without giving him access. The pilot works because acquittal is the starting pistol, not the answer.

## Freedom Arrives Before Innocence Can

The episode’s first smart move is separating the legal outcome from emotional certainty. David is acquitted after the prosecution offers no further evidence, but the writing does not let the word “free” settle anything. He says his imprisonment followed forensic negligence and a police investigation that bent evidence. He also wants his wife’s real killer found and the people who lied brought to book.

That gives the pilot a clean spine. David has won in court, but he has not won the room. The episode understands the gap. An acquittal can open a prison door without repairing a family, a public record, or a child’s trust. David’s media-facing demand for justice is direct, but it also creates pressure. The hour does not allow him to be a quiet victim. Every statement becomes a fresh demand on people who are not ready to give him anything.

The restraint helps. The episode does not rush to sanctify him. It lets his claim sit beside the unease his release creates, which is sharper than a victory lap. The pilot’s strongest idea is simple: freedom is official, innocence is social, and David has only been granted one of them.

## A Restart With Clean Hands

**DCI Beech** gives the investigation its practical reset when he orders **DI Hudson** to choose a team with no connection to the original case. The instruction matters because it admits, without a speech, that the previous process is contaminated. If David is right about forensic negligence and bent evidence, the new inquiry cannot tidy up paperwork. It has to treat the old case as part of the crime scene.

The home-office pressure around Beech adds useful institutional squeeze. This is not one detective chasing a hunch in a vacuum. The system that helped produce the conviction now needs a second version of itself to examine the first. That gives the police material a sturdy procedural hook. The episode uses dialogue density well here, especially around operational directives and case-file movement. People talk because the machine has to restart, and the restart has rules.

The pivot back toward Mr. Collins, including **Alice Moffatt**, is a smart choice because it keeps the pilot from becoming a straight exoneration drama. A weaker hour would declare David cleared and hunt only outward. This one keeps looking at the people already in the frame. That does not make David guilty. It makes the new investigation credible. Clean hands matter only if they are willing to touch the same dirt.

## Rob’s Safety Plan Starts Eating Itself

The family material is where the pilot finds its bite. **Rob** wants to protect the children from David gaining access, but the contradiction sits inside his own position. He recognizes that David’s access is inevitable and must be handled, yet he resists the dialogue and process that would make it manageable. His safety plan depends on control. The episode’s point is that control has already failed.

The rejection of the sister-in-law taking the children lands because it turns trust into a practical question. Once the couple learn she told police lies about David, her role cannot remain sentimental. The episode is asking who helped build the story that kept David away, and what those choices did to the children left behind.

This is also where the pilot shows one of its limits. Rob’s fear is clear, and the contradiction is strong, but the hour leans on position more than texture. He is defined sharply by what he opposes. The episode gives less room to how he arrived there beyond the immediate threat of David’s return. The result is effective, if blunt. Rob functions as a wall, and a wall is dramatic until the show needs to know what it is made of.

## The Missing Child Turns Procedure Into Panic

The Jack beat is the pilot’s best escalation because it moves the argument from courtrooms and case files into a family’s nervous system. When the family learns **Jack** has not been home since school, everything Rob has tried to manage becomes immediate. No one is debating access in theory now. A child is missing, and the fear used to justify resistance finally has an object.

The timing is clean. The episode establishes David’s release, then the police restart, then the access anxiety, and only then makes absence the event. That order matters. Jack’s disappearance would feel cheap if it arrived before the hour had built the family’s fear. Here, the panic pays off the earlier conversations. The family’s precautions do not look foolish. They look insufficient.

The pauses before major transitions help this section breathe. A missing-child twist can turn noisy if everyone sprints at once. The pilot gives panic enough space to register before it weaponizes it. The open loop is obvious, but productive. Whether Jack has been taken, and by whom, becomes the question that tests every claim made earlier. David wants his children back. Rob wants them safe. The episode removes certainty from both men.

## Tom Brings the Accusation Home

Then **Tom** enters the house, and the hour chooses a nastier final shape. His confrontation does not clarify the case. It dirties it. His question to David, “were you just fucking my wife, or did you kill her too?” does three things at once. It introduces another intimate allegation, links sex and murder in the same breath, and suggests David’s past may have more doors than the pilot has opened.

That is an effective cliffhanger because it changes the temperature instead of simply adding information. The police restart asks what happened that night. Tom’s accusation asks what kind of man David was around other people’s marriages, and whether the moral uncertainty around him extends beyond the conviction. The show is careful here. It does not need to answer the accusation yet. It only needs to make David’s release feel less clean.

Still, the late arrival has a cost. The confrontation is potent, but it arrives with limited runway inside the episode. As a last-scene blade, it cuts. As character drama, it is still mostly handle. The pilot earns the shock through atmosphere, but the next hour has work to do if Tom is going to become more than a man carrying a loaded line into someone else’s house.

## The Verdict

"Episode 1" is a sturdy, tense opener built around a smart refusal: it will not confuse acquittal with peace. The writing gives David a righteous demand, gives the police a reason to reopen the machinery, and gives the family a fear that turns practical when Jack goes missing. Its best craft move is structural. Every institution that should provide certainty produces another question.

The hour has flaws. Rob’s opposition can feel more functional than fully shaded, and Tom’s final accusation is more explosive than developed at this stage. But the pilot knows what it is doing. It plants its open loops cleanly, keeps the investigation under pressure, and turns a courtroom release into a domestic threat. BollyAI's score: 7.4 out of 10. In season-arc terms, this is a strong ignition point, with enough moral smoke to make the restart matter.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The cold open drops the viewer into the disorientation alongside Park Jung-woo: a prosecutor in a prison cell, charges he cannot remember, a execution date approaching. The premise is established with economy and the first episode earns its hook - what happened in that gap is a genuine puzzle.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Park Jung-woo waking up in a death row cell, unable to account for a single night that apparently destroyed his entire life.

verdict.one_liner: A tense opener turns acquittal into fresh danger, though its sharpest family conflicts still need deeper shading.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 18
episode_reviews.review_body: Defendant's finale achieves a 26.6 percent nationwide rating - the series' peak and a figure that confirmed the show had retained and grown its audience across all eighteen episodes. The resolution delivers the legal and personal reckoning with a directness that the sustained tension of the preceding seventeen episodes earned: the gap in memory that opened Episode 1, the prosecution's unexplained charges, the family's fate - all of these receive answers in the finale without the deflation that mystery payoffs frequently produce. Ji Sung's performance across the finale was identified by Korean reviewers as the series' performance peak: a man who has spent seventeen episodes operating without full knowledge of who he is now confronting the complete truth of what happened. The show confirmed its position as one of the most watched Korean legal thrillers in SBS history.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale closes out the legal and personal reckoning with a directness the series earned through its sustained tension. Audience engagement peaked here - the finale's 26.6 percent nationwide rating confirmed the show had locked in its viewers across 18 weeks and delivered enough payoff to justify the investment.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The full truth of what happened that night finally laid bare - the gap in memory that opened episode one filled in at last.
